methods.add_block:
add_block(self, identifier: str, section_id: str = '') -> dict

Adds a block to the notebook from its function identifier, "identifier" - one
of the strings list_available_blocks() returns, such as "sphere<point,real>".

Pass "section_id" to put the block in that section; left out, it lands in the
notebook's first section. Either way this moves the notebook cursor to the end
of that section, just as adding the block by hand would.

Returns a dict with three keys: "name" (the block's display name), "id" (the
handle every other method uses to refer to this block, such as delete_block()
or set_block_input() - and which is also the block's name, so it changes if
the block is renamed), and "funcId" (the identifier that was passed in).
Always use the returned "id" rather than a name you expected: if another block
with that name already exists, the notebook gives the new one a distinct one.
methods.add_section:
add_section(self, section_name: str, before_section_id: str = '') -> dict

Adds a new, empty section named "section_name" to the notebook.

Pass "before_section_id" - one of the ids list_sections() reports - to insert
the new section immediately before that one; left out, the new section is
appended at the end.

Returns a dict with the same "name" and "id" keys list_sections() returns,
describing the new section - keep hold of "id" to add blocks to it later.
Every section that already existed keeps its own id, whichever way the new
one was placed.

Raises if "before_section_id" is given but does not name a section in the
notebook.
methods.add_variable:
add_variable(self, new_name: str, block_id: str = '') -> dict

Adds a variable named "new_name" to the notebook - the console equivalent of
right-clicking a block and choosing "Make Variable".

Pass "block_id" to wrap that block in the new variable: the block itself stays
where it is and becomes the variable's contents, and anything that referenced
it goes through the variable instead. "block_id" need not be a top-level
block - one nested inside another block's input can be wrapped too. Passing
the id of a variable already in the notebook is allowed as well, and wraps it
in a new variable the same way, except that the wrapped variable keeps its own
place in the notebook in addition to becoming the new variable's contents.

Left out, an empty variable is created instead, with nothing wired into it.

Returns a dict with the same "name", "id" and "funcId" keys add_block()
returns, describing the new variable - "id" is "new_name".

Raises if "new_name" is empty, if "new_name" is already used by another block
or variable in the notebook, or if "block_id" is given but names no block.
methods.append_to_list:
append_to_list(self, source_block_id: str, target_block_id: str, target_list_id: str) -> None

Appends the block "source_block_id" into the first free slot of the list input
"target_list_id" of the block "target_block_id" - "target_list_id" is one of
the names list_block_inputs() reports for the target, whose type reads as
"list<...>".

Either block may be a top-level block or one nested inside another block's
input. The value placed is the source block itself, not one of its
properties.

Raises if "source_block_id" or "target_block_id" does not exist, if
"target_list_id" does not name an input of the target, if that input is not a
list, if it holds no list to append to (an optional list that was never
created, for instance), or if the source's type does not belong in that list -
the same check the UI's drag-and-drop makes, refusing a mismatched type or a
cycle for the same reason the UI would.
methods.block_state:
block_state(self, block_id: str) -> dict

Returns the build state of the block named by "block_id" as a dict with keys
"blockId" (the id passed in), "buildState" and "pauseState", and, only when
the block is in error, "error".

Unlike list_blocks() and delete_block(), "block_id" need not name a top-level
block - a block nested inside another block's input can be asked about too.

"buildState" is one of "e_OK", "e_UNBUILDABLE", "e_DIRTY", "e_QUEUED",
"e_BUILDING", "e_FAILED" or "e_WEAK". "pauseState" is one of "e_UNPAUSED",
"e_PAUSED" or "e_RUN_ONCE". When "buildState" is "e_FAILED", "error" holds the
same user-facing error message the notebook shows for that block.

Raises if no block with that id exists in the notebook.
methods.clear_block_input:
clear_block_input(self, block_id: str, parameter_name: str) -> None

Clears "parameter_name" of the block "block_id" - the console's version of
selecting an input and pressing Delete. "block_id" may be a top-level block or
one nested inside another block's input, the same reach connect_block_property()
has.

What becomes of what the input held depends on what was in it: a block sitting
in the input is moved back out to the top level of the notebook, appearing
just above the block it was feeding - the undo of connecting with an empty
property name, or of append_to_list(). A reference - a variable, or a
property - is simply dropped; the variable or the property's block stays
where it is.

Clearing an input that is already empty, or one still holding the default
value its block arrived with, is a success rather than a failure - a default
is deliberately left alone rather than emptied - so this can be called ahead
of connect_block_property() without checking what was there first.

Raises if "block_id" does not exist, or if "parameter_name" does not name a
parameter present on it.
methods.close_current_open_custom_block:
close_current_open_custom_block(self) -> None

Closes the custom block open_custom_block() opened, switching the console's
view back to the notebook's own main buffer - the undo of open_custom_block().

Raises if no custom block is currently open.
methods.connect_block_property:
connect_block_property(self, source_block_id: str, property_name: str, target_block_id: str, parameter_name: str) -> None

Connects a property of one block to a parameter of another - the console's
version of dragging a property chip onto an input.

"property_name" names a property of the block "source_block_id" - one of the
names list_block_properties() reports for it - and is fed into the parameter
"parameter_name" of the block "target_block_id" - one of the names
list_block_inputs() reports for it. Leave "property_name" empty to connect the
source block's own output instead of one of its named properties.

Either block may be a top-level block or one nested inside another block's
input.

Raises if "source_block_id" or "target_block_id" does not exist, if
"property_name" is non-empty and not a property the source block offers (its
type must also be known - it must have built at least once), or if
"parameter_name" does not name a parameter of the target block.
methods.current_open_custom_block:
current_open_custom_block(self) -> dict

Returns the custom block open_custom_block() last opened, as a dict with the
same "name", "id" and "bufferId" keys list_custom_blocks() returns for it.

If no custom block is currently open - the console is looking at the
notebook's own main buffer - "name" and "id" come back as empty strings and
"bufferId" as 0, rather than this raising.
methods.delete_block:
delete_block(self, block_id: str) -> dict

Deletes the block named by "block_id" - one of the ids list_blocks() reports -
and returns its description as it was just before removal, as a dict with the
same "name", "id" and "funcId" keys add_block() returns, so you have a record
of what was removed.

Only a top-level block can be named this way, the same set list_blocks()
reports; a block nested inside another block's input is not reachable here.
Raises an error if "block_id" does not name such a block.
methods.delete_variable:
delete_variable(self, block_id: str) -> dict

Deletes the variable named by "block_id" - one of the ids list_variables()
reports - and returns its description as it was just before removal, as a
dict with the same "name", "id" and "funcId" keys add_block() returns, so you
have a record of what was removed.

Only a variable can be named this way; an ordinary block answering to that id
is removed with delete_block() instead. Raises if "block_id" names an
ordinary block rather than a variable, or if it names neither.
methods.export_as_recipe:
export_as_recipe(self, recipe_path: str, recipe_only: bool = False) -> None

Exports the notebook as a JSON recipe to "recipe_path" - the Export Notebook
action. A path not already ending in ".json" gains that extension; an
existing file is overwritten without confirmation.

Pass "recipe_only" as True to write the recipe alone; left False (the
default), the extended form is written, carrying the notebook's custom blocks
and other state alongside the recipe.

If a custom block is currently open for editing - see open_custom_block() and
current_open_custom_block() - that is what gets exported, not the notebook
itself; check current_open_custom_block() beforehand if that matters.

Raises if "recipe_path" is empty, if its directory does not exist, or if a
non-file already sits at that path.
methods.get_block_input:
get_block_input(self, block_id: str, parameter_name: str) -> object

Gets the value of a block's input, in the same shape set_block_input() would
take to set it: a number for a "real", a two-item list for a "vector" or
"point", and the plain Python bool/int/str for a "bool", "integer" or "text".
Speaks in whatever unit the parameter already carries - the one
get_block_input_units() reports - rather than converting to anything else.

A parameter that has never been given a value returns None rather than
raising.

Looks through a chain of variables to find "parameter_name": a parameter the
named block does not have itself is looked for on the block it wraps, and on
that block's own content in turn while each is another variable, stopping at
the first block that is not one. So a variable made from a sphere answers to
"Radius" just as the sphere does.

Raises if "block_id" or "parameter_name" does not exist, or if the parameter
is of a type not supported here.
methods.get_block_input_units:
get_block_input_units(self, block_id: str, parameter_name: str) -> str

Gets the unit a given block's input is read and written in, as shown in the
notebook beside that input.  This is the unit the values from get_block_input()
are in, and the one set_block_input() expects.

The unit is a property of the input, not of what is in it, so this answers
for an input that has no value yet just as readily as for one that does. A
"bool", "integer" or "text" parameter carries no unit, and neither does a
"real" declared as taking a bare ratio; each of those returns an empty string
rather than raising.

Looks through a chain of variables to find "parameter_name", the same way
get_block_input() and set_block_input() do: a parameter the named block does
not have itself is looked for on the block it wraps, and so on while each is
another variable.

Raises if "block_id" or "parameter_name" does not exist.
methods.import_recipe:
import_recipe(self, recipe_path: str) -> None

Imports the JSON recipe at "recipe_path" into the notebook - the Import
Recipe action.

This adds to the notebook rather than replacing it: the recipe's blocks join
the ones already there, and its inputs are added after the existing ones.
Only the notebook's name and description are taken from the recipe. Call
new_notebook() first for a clean slate. The import lands as a single undo
step, exactly as it does from the menu.

Raises if "recipe_path" is empty, does not exist, is not a file, cannot be
read, or does not hold a readable recipe - checked before the notebook is
touched, so a refused import leaves it as it was.
methods.list_available_blocks:
list_available_blocks(self, mask: str = '') -> list[str]

Lists the identifiers of the blocks that can be added to the open notebook - the
same list the notebook's own add-block search offers, and anything it returns
can be passed straight to add_block().

An identifier is a string like "sphere<point,real>".  Some carry namespaces or 
version suffixes such as "sphere<point,real>".

Pass "mask" to filter the list to identifiers containing it as plain text,
matched case sensitively as a substring rather than as a wildcard pattern:
"sphere" and "phere" will match "sphere<point,real>", but "Sphere" and
"Sph*" will not. Left out, every available identifier is returned - a long
list, typically hundreds of entries, depending on licence and which custom
blocks the notebook has loaded.
methods.list_block_inputs:
list_block_inputs(self, id: str) -> list[dict]

Lists the parameters of the block named by "id" - one of the ids list_blocks()
reports - as a list of dicts, one per parameter, each with keys "name" (the
name to pass as "parameter_name" to set_block_input(), get_block_input(),
clear_block_input() and connect_block_property()), "type" (what it holds -
"real", "point", "vector", and many others), and "isReturnValue".

The last entry always has "isReturnValue" set to True and describes the
block's own output rather than an input - it is named after the block's id,
and is not something that can be set. Every other entry has "isReturnValue"
set to False.

This reports only the parameters the named block declares itself - it does
not look through a variable to the block it wraps, unlike set_block_input()
and get_block_input(). A block with no origin function (an orphan instance)
reports only its output, with no inputs.
methods.list_block_properties:
list_block_properties(self, block_id: str) -> list[dict]

Lists the named pieces of the output the block named by "block_id" produces -
not its inputs, which list_block_inputs() reports - as a list of dicts, one
per property, each with keys "name" (what to pass as "property_name" to
connect_block_property()) and "type".

Properties belong to the type a block's output is, not to the block itself,
so two blocks that produce the same type offer the same properties, in the
order the type declares them. "block_id" need not be a top-level block - one
nested inside another block's input can be asked about too.

A block whose output type is not yet known - one that has never built -
reports no properties rather than raising. Raises if "block_id" does not name
a block in the notebook.
methods.list_blocks:
list_blocks(self, section_id: str = '') -> list[dict]

Lists the top-level blocks in the section named by "section_id"; left out,
the notebook's first section is used.

Only blocks sitting at the top level of the section are reported - once a
block is plugged into another block's input it stops appearing here, though
it can still be reached by id.

Returns a list of dicts, one per block, each with the same three keys
add_block() returns: "name" (the block's display name), "id" (the handle
every other method uses to refer to this block), and "funcId" (the function
identifier it was created from).
methods.list_custom_blocks:
list_custom_blocks(self) -> list[dict]

Lists the custom (compound) blocks defined in the notebook - the same ones
that appear alongside built-in blocks in list_available_blocks() and can be
instanced with add_block().

Returns a list of dicts, one per custom block, each with keys "name" (its
display name - pass this, not "id", to open_custom_block()), "id" (its
function identifier, the string add_block() takes to add an instance of it),
and "bufferId" (an internal handle to the buffer the block was found in).
methods.list_sections:
list_sections(self) -> list[dict]

Lists the sections of the notebook, in the order they appear there. Every
block lives in one.

Returns a list of dicts, one per section, each with keys "name" (the
section's title, as shown in the notebook) and "id" (the handle
add_section(), add_block() and list_blocks() take to mean this section - use
this, not "name", to refer to a section elsewhere).

There is no method to remove a section; delete one in the notebook panel
itself if needed.
methods.list_variables:
list_variables(self) -> list[dict]

Lists every variable in the notebook, wherever it sits - unlike list_blocks(),
this is not limited to the top level of a section.

Returns a list of dicts, one per variable, each carrying the same "name", "id"
and "funcId" keys add_block() returns plus one more, "blockFuncId": the
function identifier of the block wrapped inside the variable, which is what
tells one variable from another since every variable's own "funcId" only says
which type ("core.var<real>", "core.var<sphere>", and so on) it carries. A
variable with nothing wired into it has an empty "blockFuncId".

Each variable is reported once, at the root of the notebook; a later mention
of the same variable elsewhere is a reference back to it, not a separate
entry.
methods.move_block:
move_block(self, block_id: str, targetBlockId: str, placeBefore: bool = False) -> dict

This moves the block named by "block_id" to sit next to the block named by
"targetBlockId" - the console's version of dragging a block to a new place in
the notebook. Pass "placeBefore" as True to put it immediately above the
target; left False (the default), it lands immediately below.

Both ids must name top-level blocks, the same set list_blocks() reports; a
block nested inside another block's input is neither one this can move nor one
it can be placed against. The two are checked before anything moves, so a
refused move leaves the notebook exactly as it was.

The block joins the target's section, which is what makes "above" and "below"
unambiguous at a section boundary: moving a block below the last block of a
section puts it at the end of that section, not at the start of the next one.

Nothing about the block changes but its place - it keeps its id, its inputs,
its connections and its build state, rather than being recreated where it
lands, so ids held from before the move stay good. Asking for the place it
already occupies is a success that does nothing.

Returns a dict with the same "name", "id" and "funcId" keys add_block()
returns, describing the block in its new position.

Raises if either id names no block in the notebook, if either names a block
that is not top-level, or if the two are the same block.
methods.new_notebook:
new_notebook(self) -> None

Starts a fresh, empty notebook - the same thing File > New does.

Unlike File > New there is no save prompt: any unsaved work in the notebook
that was open is discarded rather than asked about, so save first with
save_notebook() or save_notebook_as() if it is worth keeping.
methods.open_custom_block:
open_custom_block(self, name: str) -> None

Opens the custom block named "name" for editing, swapping the console's view
from the notebook's main buffer into that block's own - the same thing
double-clicking it does.

"name" is the block's display name - the "name" key list_custom_blocks()
reports, not its "id". Use current_open_custom_block() to see what is open
afterwards, and close_current_open_custom_block() to return to the notebook.

Raises if no custom block with that name exists in the notebook.
methods.open_notebook:
open_notebook(self, notebook_path: str) -> None

Opens the .ntop file at "notebook_path" - the same thing File > Open does,
less everything about it that needs a user: no file browser, and no save
prompt for either side, so any unsaved work in the notebook that was open is
discarded rather than asked about, and the new notebook is loaded even if it
turns out not to open cleanly.

Raises if "notebook_path" is empty, does not exist, is not an nTop file, or
cannot be read, or if the load fails or times out.
methods.rename_variable:
rename_variable(self, block_id: str, new_block_id: str) -> dict

Renames the variable named by "block_id" - one of the ids list_variables()
reports - to "new_block_id", since a variable's name is the id it answers to.

Returns a dict with the same "name", "id" and "funcId" keys add_block()
returns, describing the variable under its new name.

Only a variable can be renamed this way; an ordinary block answering to
"block_id" is reported as an error rather than renamed. Raises if
"new_block_id" is empty, if it is already used by another block or variable
anywhere in the notebook - even "block_id"'s own current name - or if
"block_id" names an ordinary block rather than a variable, or names neither.
methods.save_notebook:
save_notebook(self) -> None

Saves the notebook over the file it was last saved to or opened from - the
same thing File > Save does, less the alert it would raise if the write
failed.

Raises if the notebook has never been saved - there is no file to overwrite,
and picking one is save_notebook_as()'s job, not this one's - or if the save
fails or times out.
methods.save_notebook_as:
save_notebook_as(self, notebook_path: str) -> None

Saves the notebook to "notebook_path" - the same thing File > Save As does,
less everything about it that needs a user: no file browser, no confirmation
before overwriting an existing file, and no alert if the write fails.

The extension the file browser would have forced on a typed name is applied
here too, so "notebook_path" ends up with a ".ntop" extension whatever was
given.

This is also how a notebook that has never been saved gets its first path;
after it succeeds, save_notebook() saves back to "notebook_path" without
asking again.

Raises if "notebook_path" is empty, if its directory does not exist, if a
non-file already sits at that path, or if the save fails or times out.
methods.set_block_input:
set_block_input(self, block_id: str, parameter_name: str, value: object, units: str = '') -> None

Sets the input for a given block.

Looks through a chain of variables to find "parameter_name": a parameter the
named block does not have itself is looked for on the block it wraps, and so
on while each is another variable. To set the value of a scalar, vector, or
point held directly in a variable - one made with add_variable() and never
wired up to a block, such as one from add_block("core.var<real>") - name the
variable as "block_id" and pass "Input" as "parameter_name": that is the name
of the variable's own, single input.

Pass "units" to say what unit the value is in - "mm", "in", "MPa", "deg" and so
on - and it is read as being in that unit instead of in the notebook's current
units, so a value of 1 with units "in" sets one inch whatever lengths are being
displayed in.  Left out, the value is in the notebook's current units.

For a "real" parameter the unit is also recorded as what the value was written
as, so the input box shows it back as typed: 30 with units "cm" reads "30cm"
there.  A "vector" and a "point" only convert - their three boxes share one
expression and do not display it - so those go on showing the value in the
notebook's own units.

A parameter with no dimension yet - an empty one, or one holding a bare number -
takes on the unit's dimension instead of having to match it, which is how a
vector parameter comes by a dimension at all.

Only "real", "vector" and "point" parameters carry a unit; naming one for any
other type raises, as does a unit the notebook does not know, one of a different
dimension than the parameter's, one for a parameter declared to take a bare
ratio, and one named for an absolute temperature.
methods.set_block_input_units:
set_block_input_units(self, block_id: str, parameter_name: str, units: str) -> None

Records an input as being expressed in the named unit - "mm", "in", "MPa", "deg"
and so on.

A value that already has a unit keeps the quantity it is and is only rewritten,
so a length showing as 25.4mm is recorded as "1in" - which is what its box then
shows.  A value with no units is a bare number, so the unit is applied to it
instead: a 30 in the input becomes 30cm.

Works for a "real" parameter, and for a "real_field" one holding a number rather
than a computed field.  A "vector" and a "point" are refused: a parameter has
one expression to record, so there is nowhere to say that three coordinates are
each in inches.

Note that an input has nowhere to store a unit of its own - the unit values are
shown in comes from the application-wide unit settings - so this writes the text
the input records as having been typed into it, which its box redisplays.  It is
cleared if the global unit for that dimension changes.

Raises if the unit is not one the notebook knows, if it is a unit of a different
dimension than the input's, if the parameter is of any other type, if the block
declares it as taking a bare ratio, if it is an absolute temperature, or if it
holds no value.
